newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium says troops not to meddle in Zaire affairs.
newsitem.headline: Belgium says troops not to meddle in Zaire affairs.

text.p: Belgium said on Sunday that the 550 paratroopers it plans to send to its former colony Zaire will go there solely to evacuate its nationals and that it has no intentions of meddling in Zaire's affairs.

"Our ambition is to help our citizens who want to leave the country. This has no political bearing whatsoever, particularly with regard to the current regime there," Defence Minister Jean-Paul Poncelet told Belgian radio RTBF on Sunday.
France and the United States are also sending troops for a possible evacuation of their nationals from the war-torn central African country.
Zaire is in deep crisis as long-time ruler President Mobutu Sese Seko, 66, is gravely ill with cancer and rebels led by Laurent Kabila have seized about a fifth of the country.

A first group of 35 Belgian reconnaissance and liaison officers was flying to Brazzaville, the capital of neighbouring Congo across the Zaire river, late on Sunday evening. Part of that group will go to Kinshasa to protect the Belgian embassy.
The rest of the 550 soldiers who are part of the "Green Stream" operation will follow on Monday, an army spokesman told a news conference on Sunday.
"As long as it is not necessary, we will not move onto Zairean soil," an army spokesman said.
Belgian media have estimated the number of Westerners in the Zairean capital at about 7,000, including fewer than 3,000 Belgians, about 1,000 French and 650 Americans.
Belgian Foreign Minister Erik Derycke said he was annoyed by the fact that the Belgians in Zaire seemed so reluctant to leave the country, despite repeated calls to do so.

"There is a false feeling of security there. We have been saying for weeks that they have to leave. Now we have no other choice than to set up an evacuation mission again, at the taxpayer's expense," he told RTBF radio.
Some 100 Belgians flew home on Saturday with commercial flights, another 250 followed on Sunday.
"Women and children are leaving. But those who have business interests here want to stay until the last minute," Belgian diamond trader Jean-Pierre Winkler told VTM television in Zaire.
Since Zaire, formerly Belgian Congo, won independence in 1960, Belgium has repeatedly sent troops to evacuate nationals during the many crises of Mobutu's regime, most recently in 1991 and 1993.
In 1978, dozens of Europeans were killed in the Kolwezi mining centre in the Shaba province, before Belgian and French paratroopers could move in to evacuate their citizens.
Like Poncelet, Derycke stressed Belgium's latest military mission had no intention of intervening in Zaire's political affairs. But in the same breath made an opening to Kabila.
"After 35 years of Mobutu, the country is destroyed, the Zaireans have had enough of him. Zaireans want change, and change is called Kabila now," he said.
